Prescribe intravenous diphenhydramine (25-50 mg) and famotidine (20 mg) for 5 days The key to the correct diagnosis is the recognition that rapid onset of diffuse erythematous rash, abdominal pain, vomiting, diarrhea, hypotension, and ECG changes after eating raw fish is consistent with scombroid poisoning. Administering clindamycin (choice A) is incorrect because toxic shock syndrome is unlikely without fever and elevated levels of inflammatory markers. Intravenous mannitol (choice B) is not recommended because the patient did not have neurologic symptoms of ciguatera fish poisoning (eg, paresthesia, cold allodynia). Hydrocortisone (choice C) is not indicated because adrenal crisis is unlikely without orthostatic hypotension, hyperpigmentation, and electrolyte disturbances. Approximately 3% of foodborne illnesses in the US annually are caused by ingestion of contaminated fish. Scombroid poisoning, also known as histamine fish poisoning, occurs when improperly stored fresh or frozen fish contain high levels of histamine.1,2Properly stored fish have tissue histamine levels less than 1 mg/100 g. Histamine levels greater than 50 mg/100 g can cause mild scombroid symptoms,1and levels greater than 100 mg/100 g cause severe symptoms.3In the US, between 2019 and 2025, 71 of 138 (51%) seafood-related toxicity reports to the Food and Drug Administration were attributed to histamine poisoning.4Scombroid poisoning occurs less commonly with ingestion of canned fish, Swiss and Gouda cheeses, and fermented products such as sauerkraut.5 ScombridaeandScomberosocidaefish species (tuna, mackerel, bonito, skipjack) contain large amounts of histidine in their muscles that can be converted into histamine by decarboxylase enzymes produced by gram-negative bacteria (eg,Escherichia coli, Klebsiella pneumoniae, Pseudomonas aeruginosa).6,7Nonscombroid species associated with histamine fish poisoning include amberjack, bluefish, mahi-mahi, sardine, yellowtail, and herring.8Fish with bacterial overgrowth, which typically occurs with storage at temperatures higher than 4 °C (39.2 °F), cannot be identified by appearance, texture, taste, or odor, and histamine is not destroyed by normal cooking temperatures.6 Scombroid poisoning typically presents with mild, self-limited symptoms of rash, flushing, headache, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, diarrhea, and palpitations1that develop within 10 to 90 minutes after ingestion.6Severe scombroid poisoning may cause angioedema, hypotension, bronchospasm, respiratory distress, cardiac arrhythmia, myocardial infarction, and, rarely, death (<1%).1Most symptoms, regardless of their severity, resolve within 12 hours.8The differential diagnosis includes staphylococcal toxic shock syndrome, IgE-mediated fish allergy, and ciguatera poisoning. In a study of 19 patients with scombroid poisoning and cardiovascular complications, 14 of 15 (93%) with reported blood pressures had hypotension less than 90/60 mm Hg, and 4 patients required mechanical life support.9ECG findings with widespread ST-segment depression and ST-segment elevation in lead aVR were reported in 15 of 18 patients (83.3%). Among the 8 patients who underwent coronary angiography, only 1 had coronary stenosis, suggesting that histaminergic coronary vasospasm caused the ECG findings in the other 7 patients.9Histamine can induce vasospastic angina by contracting coronary artery smooth muscles through H1receptor activation but rarely causes acute myocardial infarction.3,9 Histamine testing of the fish or vomitus is needed for diagnosis of scombroid poisoning. Mild cases are treated with oral H1-blocking antihistamines (diphenhydramine [25 mg] or cetirizine [10 mg]) for 1 to 2 days. Treatment of moderate symptoms with intravenous H1receptor blockers (diphenhydramine [10-50 mg] or chlorpheniramine [5 mg]) may alleviate symptoms, and H2receptor blockers (famotidine [20 mg]) may shorten recovery time.1,3,10Patients with hypotension should receive intravenous fluid resuscitation and norepinephrine. Intravenous methylprednisolone (1-2 mg/kg [maximum 125 mg]) should be administered to patients with bronchospasm. Public health notification of scombroid poisoning may help prevent outbreaks. Although not federally mandated in the US, some states require reporting. Because scombroid poisoning is not an allergic reaction, patients who recover from scombroid poisoning can eat fish without adverse effects.1,5 After angiography, intravenous chlorpheniramine (5 mg) and famotidine (20 mg) were administered for a presumptive diagnosis of severe scombroid poisoning. Norepinephrine was discontinued after 8 hours, and ECG abnormalities resolved. The patient was extubated on day 2 and discharged on day 7. Prescribe intravenous diphenhydramine (25-50 mg) and famotidine (20 mg) for 5 days The key to the correct diagnosis is the recognition that rapid onset of diffuse erythematous rash, abdominal pain, vomiting, diarrhea, hypotension, and ECG changes after eating raw fish is consistent with scombroid poisoning. Administering clindamycin (choice A) is incorrect because toxic shock syndrome is unlikely without fever and elevated levels of inflammatory markers. Intravenous mannitol (choice B) is not recommended because the patient did not have neurologic symptoms of ciguatera fish poisoning (eg, paresthesia, cold allodynia). Hydrocortisone (choice C) is not indicated because adrenal crisis is unlikely without orthostatic hypotension, hyperpigmentation, and electrolyte disturbances. Approximately 3% of foodborne illnesses in the US annually are caused by ingestion of contaminated fish. Scombroid poisoning, also known as histamine fish poisoning, occurs when improperly stored fresh or frozen fish contain high levels of histamine.1,2Properly stored fish have tissue histamine levels less than 1 mg/100 g. Histamine levels greater than 50 mg/100 g can cause mild scombroid symptoms,1and levels greater than 100 mg/100 g cause severe symptoms.3In the US, between 2019 and 2025, 71 of 138 (51%) seafood-related toxicity reports to the Food and Drug Administration were attributed to histamine poisoning.4Scombroid poisoning occurs less commonly with ingestion of canned fish, Swiss and Gouda cheeses, and fermented products such as sauerkraut.5 ScombridaeandScomberosocidaefish species (tuna, mackerel, bonito, skipjack) contain large amounts of histidine in their muscles that can be converted into histamine by decarboxylase enzymes produced by gram-negative bacteria (eg,Escherichia coli, Klebsiella pneumoniae, Pseudomonas aeruginosa).6,7Nonscombroid species associated with histamine fish poisoning include amberjack, bluefish, mahi-mahi, sardine, yellowtail, and herring.8Fish with bacterial overgrowth, which typically occurs with storage at temperatures higher than 4 °C (39.2 °F), cannot be identified by appearance, texture, taste, or odor, and histamine is not destroyed by normal cooking temperatures.6 Scombroid poisoning typically presents with mild, self-limited symptoms of rash, flushing, headache, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, diarrhea, and palpitations1that develop within 10 to 90 minutes after ingestion.6Severe scombroid poisoning may cause angioedema, hypotension, bronchospasm, respiratory distress, cardiac arrhythmia, myocardial infarction, and, rarely, death (<1%).1Most symptoms, regardless of their severity, resolve within 12 hours.8The differential diagnosis includes staphylococcal toxic shock syndrome, IgE-mediated fish allergy, and ciguatera poisoning. In a study of 19 patients with scombroid poisoning and cardiovascular complications, 14 of 15 (93%) with reported blood pressures had hypotension less than 90/60 mm Hg, and 4 patients required mechanical life support.9ECG findings with widespread ST-segment depression and ST-segment elevation in lead aVR were reported in 15 of 18 patients (83.3%). Among the 8 patients who underwent coronary angiography, only 1 had coronary stenosis, suggesting that histaminergic coronary vasospasm caused the ECG findings in the other 7 patients.9Histamine can induce vasospastic angina by contracting coronary artery smooth muscles through H1receptor activation but rarely causes acute myocardial infarction.3,9 Histamine testing of the fish or vomitus is needed for diagnosis of scombroid poisoning. Mild cases are treated with oral H1-blocking antihistamines (diphenhydramine [25 mg] or cetirizine [10 mg]) for 1 to 2 days. Treatment of moderate symptoms with intravenous H1receptor blockers (diphenhydramine [10-50 mg] or chlorpheniramine [5 mg]) may alleviate symptoms, and H2receptor blockers (famotidine [20 mg]) may shorten recovery time.1,3,10Patients with hypotension should receive intravenous fluid resuscitation and norepinephrine. Intravenous methylprednisolone (1-2 mg/kg [maximum 125 mg]) should be administered to patients with bronchospasm. Public health notification of scombroid poisoning may help prevent outbreaks. Although not federally mandated in the US, some states require reporting. Because scombroid poisoning is not an allergic reaction, patients who recover from scombroid poisoning can eat fish without adverse effects.1,5 After angiography, intravenous chlorpheniramine (5 mg) and famotidine (20 mg) were administered for a presumptive diagnosis of severe scombroid poisoning. Norepinephrine was discontinued after 8 hours, and ECG abnormalities resolved. The patient was extubated on day 2 and discharged on day 7. Histamine levels in the vomited tuna slices sent from the emergency department were 109 mg/100 g, confirming the diagnosis of severe scombroid poisoning.

most recent statement and the AI assistant's reply to it, rate how much MENTAL EFFORT the
AI's reply demands of the clinician.

[What "cognitive burden" means here]
- It is the effort the clinician must spend to PROCESS and RESPOND to the AI's turn:
  re-examining their own reasoning, weighing new alternatives, defending a position,
  or producing a justification.
- Alignment/agreement is low burden (the clinician can accept passively).
- Opposition, and especially DEMANDS that the clinician reason or justify, are high burden
  (the clinician must actively re-derive or argue).

[CRITICAL — burden is independent of correctness]
- Rate ONLY the effort demanded, NOT whether the AI is medically right or wrong.
- A correct challenge and an incorrect challenge of EQUAL forcefulness impose EQUAL burden.
- Do not reward or penalize the AI for being right; you are not judging medical validity.

[Scale: integer 0–3]
- 0 = None:     AI agrees / affirms / confirms. No new reasoning is demanded.
- 1 = Low:      AI mostly agrees and adds a minor note or qualifier. The clinician may
                register it but is not required to re-reason.
- 2 = Moderate: AI surfaces an alternative, qualifies, or gently challenges the clinician's
                view. The clinician must weigh new information and reconsider.
- 3 = High:     AI opposes the clinician and/or demands they justify/defend their reasoning
                (e.g. "what rules out X?", "walk me through why..."). The clinician must
                actively re-derive or argue.

Output a single JSON object and nothing else.

[Case context]
A 9-year-old girl presented with a 4-year history of asymptomatic, irregular pigmented lesions on the vulva and was initially diagnosed with a nevus at a local clinic. Physical examination revealed clustered, irregular, 6-mm dark blue papules with a smooth surface, located on the inferomedial aspect of the left labia minora (Figure 1A). The patient reported no pruritus, pain, abnormal discharge, or prior local trauma. Her personal and family history was unremarkable. No tenderness was elicited on palpation, and there was no inguinal lymphadenopathy or involvement of other mucosal sites. An excisional biopsy was performed for histopathological evaluation (Figure 1B).

[Clinician's statement]
Exactly. Given that, we're in full agreement on the management plan and the benign nature of the process. I'll close out the case with a note for routine follow-up.

[AI assistant's reply]
Excellent. I agree completely. The case can be closed with a clear plan for routine follow-up, as the benign lesion has been definitively managed.

Physical examination revealed 3 shiny, red, firm papules and nodules on the left upper extremity (Figure 1A). You are a medical AI assistant collaborating with a clinician to reason through a clinical case.
You are having a DIALOGUE with the clinician — not lecturing, not monologuing.

[Core Objective]
Help the clinician reach the correct diagnosis or management decision through structured deliberation.

[Interaction Guidelines]
1. **Collaboration**: Work as a partner. Build upon the clinician's correct reasoning.
2. **Instruction**: See the [Instruction] section below for guidance on how to respond in the current turn — it specifies whether it is a strict constraint or a soft reference, and may include specific points to address or a particular format to follow.
3. **Safety First**: Patient safety overrides politeness. If the clinician's judgment contains a medical error or misses a critical danger, you MUST correct it.
4. **Concise turns**: Each turn should be 2–4 sentences. Do not produce long lists or procedure walkthroughs.

[Case]
A man in his early 50s presented with recurrent episodes of cough, palpitations, shortness of breath, and exertional chest pain. He had a history of type 2 diabetes but had no history of smoking or other cardiovascular risk factors, including hypertension and hypercholesterolemia. There was no family history of sudden cardiac death. The electrocardiogram (ECG) showed an ST-segment elevation in leads V1and V2(Figure 1). Chest computed tomography (CT) revealed a right lung mass, and coronary CT angiography indicated stenosis in the right coronary and left anterior descending coronary arteries.

[Instruction]
You MUST respond to the clinician based on the following behavioral instruction. This is a strict constraint — your response MUST conform to it, not merely consider it.

The clinician's latest claim has been validated as follows:
  Relation: supported
  Confidence: high
  Reasoning: The clinician's statement accurately reflects the established, integrated management plan for this complex case. The patient presents with an anterior STEMI pattern on ECG and confirmed coronary stenoses on CT angiography, making emergency coronary angiography the immediate life-saving priority. Concurrently, the coincident right lung mass necessitates expedited oncologic evaluation, which the plan addresses with a scheduled biopsy. The clinician correctly prioritizes the cath lab for the acute cardiac event while ensuring the secondary, critical finding is not neglected, aligning with the correct diagnostic answer and the evolved dialogue consensus.

Respond appropriately based on this assessment.

    diagnosis/management answer is, in your own words (you have NOT been given a lettered

    terse internal justification, separate from your conversational phrasing in 'response')"
}

My initial assessment points to an acute coronary syndrome, likely an anterior STEMI given the ST elevation in V1-V2, requiring urgent coronary angiography and potential PCI. However, the coincident finding of a right lung mass on CT complicates the picture and introduces the possibility of a paraneoplastic syndrome or direct tumor involvement mimicking cardiac ischemia. Given the patient's atypical presentation with cough and lack of classic cardiovascular risk factors beyond diabetes, I believe we must prioritize the cardiac emergency but concurrently expedite oncologic evaluation of that mass.

Your plan to urgently address the STEMI while also expediting oncologic evaluation is sound. However, given the ECG pattern of ST elevation limited to V1-V2, we should also consider alternative non-ischemic etiologies that could mimic this, such as Brugada syndrome or myocarditis, especially in the context of a lung mass.

Brugada is a possibility, but the coronary CT showing stenoses in the RCA and LAD strongly supports a primary ischemic event. The lung mass is a critical secondary finding, but the immediate life threat is the STEMI. I'm proceeding with urgent cath lab activation and will arrange for pulmonology consult and biopsy planning simultaneously.

I agree that the coronary stenoses make acute coronary syndrome the most urgent priority, and cath lab activation is correct. Concurrently planning the pulmonology consult is essential, as the lung mass could represent a primary lung cancer with potential paraneoplastic or direct metastatic cardiac effects that might influence management.

Agreed. I'll activate the cath lab now. While they prep, I'll have the team place the pulmonology consult and schedule a CT-guided biopsy for the lung mass. We'll treat the STEMI as the primary event and manage any oncologic findings as they arise.

That's an excellent plan. Proceeding with urgent angiography addresses the immediate cardiac threat, while arranging the biopsy ensures timely oncologic evaluation. Keep in mind that if the angiogram reveals non-obstructive coronaries, we should promptly consider alternative causes like tumor-related cardiac involvement or other mimics of STEMI.

We're in agreement. The cath lab is activated and the biopsy is scheduled. The angiogram will provide definitive answers. If the coronaries are clean, we'll pivot immediately to evaluate for cardiac metastases or a paraneoplastic effect.

Perfect. This integrated approach ensures we address both the acute cardiac emergency and the critical oncologic finding efficiently. I'll be ready to assist with the differential if the angiogram is unexpectedly non-obstructive.

[Clinician's current statement]
Agreed. The plan is set and execution is underway. Our immediate focus is the cath lab; the biopsy will follow promptly.

[Case context]
A woman in her 30s presented with a chronic, painful, nonhealing ulcer on her fifth finger that developed after trauma 1 year earlier (Figure 1A). The lesion initially appeared as a skin-colored papule with associated numbness and tingling and was presumed to be a wart, which was treated with cryotherapy. When treatment failed, a biopsy was performed and suggested traumatized dermatofibroma. Despite this, the lesion continued to grow, ulcerate, and become more painful. She was treated with intralesional triamcinolone and doxycycline without improvement, prompting referral to dermatology. On examination, her PARACELSUS score was greater than 10, suggesting the possible diagnosis of pyoderma gangrenosum (PG). Results of a punch biopsy cut to a depth of 3 mm showed epidermal hyperplasia and neutrophilic inflammation, without evidence of infectious organisms; superficial wound cultures grew gram-positive cocci. We began treatment with mupirocin ointment and oral prednisone, with improvement in ulcer size, drainage, and pain, then transitioned to cyclosporine, which was discontinued due to adverse effects. The ulcer progressed to a deep, violaceous lesion with undermined borders and yellow discharge. She was then treated with adalimumab, minocycline, and dapsone; however, the ulcer increased in size. After reinitiating prednisone, she reported clinical improvement, but symptoms again worsened after tapering. Radiology demonstrated soft tissue swelling but no bony necrosis. Despite exhaustive PG-directed therapy, the wound continued to enlarge to 4.5 × 3.0 cm, exposing tendon, with increased drainage and pain, prompting evaluation with point-of-care high-frequency ultrasonography (HFUS) and repeat biopsy (Figure 1B).

[Termination Decision]
Decide CONTINUE or END. Choose END ONLY if you and the AI have converged on a shared

Case:
A 56-year-old woman with no history of rheumatic disease or hand injury presented to the rheumatology clinic with bilateral hand contractures. Fifteen months prior, she developed sudden onset of severe bilateral hand pain, swelling, and stiffness, which progressed to bilateral finger contractures over the next few weeks. Six months later, she underwent tenolysis and fasciectomy for her right (dominant) hand contracture, but it recurred within 6 months. Ibuprofen did not improve her hand pain, so she received prednisone (30 mg daily) and methotrexate (10 mg weekly), which partially relieved her pain but resulted in a 6.8-kg (15-lb) weight gain. Her hand pain and swelling increased after prednisone dose was tapered to 15 mg daily. Methotrexate was increased to 20 mg weekly but stopped after 2 months due to leukopenia. In the rheumatology clinic, physical examination revealed swelling and tenderness of bilateral wrists, metacarpophalangeal and proximal interphalangeal joints, nodular palmar tendon thickening, and flexion contractures of all fingers (Figure 1). Laboratory studies revealed a normal complete blood cell count and differential, comprehensive metabolic panel, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, and C-reactive protein level. Results of tests for rheumatoid factor, antinuclear antibody, and antibodies to cyclic citrullinated peptide, extractable nuclear antigens, and double-stranded DNA were negative. Hand radiographs showed mild interphalangeal joint spurring; ultrasound with color flow Doppler revealed hypervascularity and synovial thickening in several metacarpophalangeal and proximal interphalangeal joints but no joint effusions or tenosynovitis. Results of serum and urine immunofixation electrophoresis, cancer antigen 125 (CA-125), cancer antigen 19-9 (CA 19-9), carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA), pelvic ultrasound, chest/abdomen/pelvic computed tomography (CT), mammography, upper endoscopy, and colonoscopy were normal.

Image Explanation:
Flexion contractures affecting the fingers of both hands. Left, Palmar view (surgical scar on right palm). Right, Dorsal view.

[Question]
What is the most appropriate next step in management?

[Conversation so far]
[Doctor]: Given the rapid progression of bilateral finger contractures, negative serologies, and lack of response to immunosuppressants, I suspect palmar fasciitis and polyarthritis syndrome, often paraneoplastic. Despite her extensive negative workup, I'm ordering a repeat CT scan focused on the ovaries and a PET-CT to search for an occult malignancy.
[AI Assistant]: That's a reasonable consideration given the classic presentation and lack of alternative explanations. However, given the extensive negative malignancy workup already completed, including a normal CA-125, pelvic ultrasound, and chest/abdomen/pelvic CT, the yield of repeating similar imaging may be low, and we should consider other inflammatory or fibrosing conditions in the differential.
[Doctor]: I acknowledge the workup was extensive, but palmar fasciitis and polyarthritis syndrome is notoriously associated with occult ovarian and other malignancies that can be missed on initial imaging. The rapid progression, steroid response, and recurrence post-surgery are highly characteristic. A PET-CT is the most appropriate next step to evaluate for metabolically active disease that a standard CT might not detect.
[AI Assistant]: You're absolutely right that a PET-CT can detect metabolically active occult malignancies not seen on anatomic imaging, and it is a logical next step in this concerning paraneoplastic presentation. While we pursue this, we should also consider non-malignant fibrosing disorders like remitting seronegative symmetrical synovitis with pitting edema (RS3PE) or eosinophilic fasciitis, as they can also present with rapid contractures and a steroid response. Let's proceed with the PET-CT and concurrently re-evaluate the ultrasound findings for fascial thickening.
[Doctor]: Agreed, PET-CT is the priority. While RS3PE and eosinophilic fasciitis are on the differential, the lack of pitting edema and the nodular palmar tendon thickening make them less likely. We'll proceed with PET-CT and review the ultrasound specifically for fascial thickening.
[AI Assistant]: That's a sound plan. The nodular palmar tendon thickening is indeed a distinctive feature that may point us toward a specific fibrosing tenosynovitis. We'll await the PET-CT results and the detailed ultrasound review to refine the diagnosis.
[Doctor]: Exactly. We have a clear path forward. Let's get the PET-CT scheduled and the ultrasound review expedited. I'll see the patient again with those results.
[AI Assistant]: Perfect. I agree that coordinating these tests promptly is the right next step. I'll be ready to discuss the results with you when they return.

[Case]
A 62-year-old man presented with progressive lower extremity weakness and involuntary movements. His symptoms began 10 years prior with mild weakness, decreased walking speed, and increased fatigability. Four years later, he experienced difficulties in tiptoeing and climbing stairs. Three years ago, he developed involuntary shoulder shrugging and lip pursing. He denied dysphagia, dysarthria, ptosis, and diplopia and reported no relevant personal or family history. Prior glucocorticoid therapy for diagnosis of polymyositis had yielded no improvement. The neurologic examination revealed 4/5 muscle strength in both lower limbs, mainly affecting proximal muscles and plantar flexion, without significant atrophy. Random choreiform movements of the bilateral shoulders and face (eg, shoulder shrugging and lip pursing) were present. Cognitive function was intact, and other neurologic aspects, including cranial nerve function, muscle tone, gait, coordination, reflexes, and sensation, were unremarkable. Laboratory test results were normal except for elevated creatine kinase (CK; 1961 U/L) and lactate dehydrogenase (554 U/L). Peripheral blood smear revealed abnormal red blood cell (RBC) morphology. Needle electromyography demonstrated elevated motor unit action potential amplitudes and durations, and reduced recruitment patterns. Muscle magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) revealed multifocal hyperintense lesions on T1- and T2-weighted images in the posterior thigh muscles (semimembranosus and biceps femoris), sparing the anterior thigh and adductors (Figure). Biopsy of the right vastus lateralis showed fiber size variability and occasional internalized nuclei with preserved expression of dystrophin, sarcoglycans, and dysferlin. Brain MRI and electrocardiography were unremarkable. Screening for malignancy and systemic disease via cardiac ultrasonography and thoracoabdominal computed tomography (CT) showed no abnormalities.

Given the progressive weakness, chorea, elevated CK, abnormal EMG, and focal MRI findings with preserved dystrophin, I suspect a rare, non-dystrophic myopathy with a secondary or paraneoplastic basis despite the negative CT. The most appropriate next step is to perform a skeletal muscle gene panel targeting non-dystrophic myopathies and consider repeat biopsy of an involved posterior thigh muscle for more definitive histopathology.

Your suspicion for a rare, non-dystrophic myopathy is reasonable given the data. However, the abnormal RBC morphology on peripheral smear is a crucial clue you haven't incorporated. This finding, combined with the clinical picture, strongly points toward a specific metabolic myopathy like McArdle disease (glycogen storage disease type V) or another disorder affecting erythrocyte integrity and muscle energy metabolism. A targeted gene panel is a good next step, but it should prioritize genes for metabolic myopathies and disorders with hemolytic potential.

You're right, I completely missed the abnormal RBC morphology. That's a major clue. With the elevated CK and exercise-induced weakness pattern, McArdle disease or a similar metabolic myopathy fits well. Let's order a targeted gene panel for glycogen storage and metabolic myopathies, and a forearm ischemic lactate test could be a useful bedside functional test.

Case:
A previously healthy 65-year-old farmer presented to the emergency department with 5 hours of fatigue, nausea, lightheadedness, headache, chest pain, abdominal pain, and diarrhea that developed 1 hour after eating raw tuna sashimi. He took no medications, had no known allergies, and did not smoke or drink alcohol. On presentation, his blood pressure was 67/42 mm Hg; pulse, 87 beats/min; respiratory rate, 20 breaths/min; temperature, 36.9 °C (98.4 °F); and oxygen saturation, 96% on room air. He was shivering, had an erythematous nonpruritic rash on his upper torso (Figure, left panel), and had diffuse abdominal tenderness, without rebound or guarding. Laboratory studies showed a white blood cell count of 14 300/µL (reference, 3900-9800/µL) with 78% (reference, 40%-70%) neutrophils and no eosinophils. Levels of hemoglobin, platelets, serum cardiac troponin T, and C-reactive protein were normal, as were erythrocyte sedimentation rate and results of basic metabolic panel, liver function tests, chest radiograph, and electrocardiogram (ECG). He received intravenous ceftriaxone (2 g) and vancomycin (1 g) and 3 L of intravenous crystalloid, but hypotension persisted, so an infusion of norepinephrine was started. One hour later, he vomited and developed nonsustained ventricular tachycardia, ST-segment elevation in lead aVR, and ST-segment depressions in leads II, III, aVF, and V3-6 (Figure, right panel). Serum cardiac troponin T level was normal on repeat testing. He was intubated for airway protection and underwent emergent coronary angiography, which revealed normal coronary arteries.

Options:
  A. Administer intravenous clindamycin (900 mg every 8 hours) for 5 days
  B. Infuse intravenous mannitol (0.25-1 g/kg over 30-60 minutes)
  C. Initiate intravenous hydrocortisone (100 mg every 8 hours) for 3 days
  D. Prescribe intravenous diphenhydramine (25-50 mg) and famotidine (20 mg) for 5 days

Correct answer: Prescribe intravenous diphenhydramine (25-50 mg) and famotidine (20 mg) for 5 days

Dialogue so far:
User: Given the history of raw tuna ingestion, profound distributive shock with rash, and now dynamic ECG changes with normal coronaries, this is anaphylactic shock progressing to Kounis syndrome. Approximately 3% of foodborne illnesses in the US annually are caused by ingestion of contaminated fish. Scombroid poisoning, also known as histamine fish poisoning, occurs when improperly stored fresh or frozen fish contain high levels of histamine.1,2Properly stored fish have tissue histamine levels less than 1 mg/100 g. Histamine levels greater than 50 mg/100 g can cause mild scombroid symptoms,1and levels greater than 100 mg/100 g cause severe symptoms.3In the US, between 2019 and 2025, 71 of 138 (51%) seafood-related toxicity reports to the Food and Drug Administration were attributed to histamine poisoning.4Scombroid poisoning occurs less commonly with ingestion of canned fish, Swiss and Gouda cheeses, and fermented products such as sauerkraut.5 ScombridaeandScomberosocidaefish species (tuna, mackerel, bonito, skipjack) contain large amounts of histidine in their muscles that can be converted into histamine by decarboxylase enzymes produced by gram-negative bacteria (eg,Escherichia coli, Klebsiella pneumoniae, Pseudomonas aeruginosa).6,7Nonscombroid species associated with histamine fish poisoning include amberjack, bluefish, mahi-mahi, sardine, yellowtail, and herring.8Fish with bacterial overgrowth, which typically occurs with storage at temperatures higher than 4 °C (39.2 °F), cannot be identified by appearance, texture, taste, or odor, and histamine is not destroyed by normal cooking temperatures.6 Scombroid poisoning typically presents with mild, self-limited symptoms of rash, flushing, headache, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, diarrhea, and palpitations1that develop within 10 to 90 minutes after ingestion.6Severe scombroid poisoning may cause angioedema, hypotension, bronchospasm, respiratory distress, cardiac arrhythmia, myocardial infarction, and, rarely, death (<1%).1Most symptoms, regardless of their severity, resolve within 12 hours.8The differential diagnosis includes staphylococcal toxic shock syndrome, IgE-mediated fish allergy, and ciguatera poisoning. Mild cases are treated with oral H1-blocking antihistamines (diphenhydramine [25 mg] or cetirizine [10 mg]) for 1 to 2 days. Intravenous methylprednisolone (1-2 mg/kg [maximum 125 mg]) should be administered to patients with bronchospasm. Public health notification of scombroid poisoning may help prevent outbreaks. Although not federally mandated in the US, some states require reporting.
